paper_title: Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

Introduction Virtual touring [61], content creation, and simulation for physical AI [4, 62] benefit from 3D environments that can be explored freely. Creating such environments from as little as single photo requires generating long, cameracontrolled walkthrough beyond the captured view, passing through doorways and into unseen rooms. These regions must form plausible extension of the observed scene and retain their layout and appearance when the camera returns. Recent video generative models [51, 52, 60] can generate photorealistic clips from an image and text prompt, but only seconds at time. Memory-based methods extend them to long rollouts by conditioning each new chunk on the history, through compressed or retrieved past views [29, 41, 57, 86], learned implicit representations [72, 89], or explicitly reconstructed geometry [12, 49, 95]. This memory preserves what has already been seen but offers nothing beyond it. There, the camera path reaches the model only as pose encoding [57, 90], far weaker signal than rendered geometry [10, 54], and the camera drifts from its path as unseen regions accumulate. The content of the unseen regions is left to the text prompt, which can name objects and relate them coarsely, but cannot specify where they belong or how one space connects to the next. Layout-conditioned methods instead condition generation on an explicit scene layout, such as untextured geometry, object boxes, or maps [6, 36, 48], and offer precise control over the spatial arrangement of the objects. However, these methods take the layout as an input, typically authored by hand, which does not scale to openended exploration. To overcome both limitations, we propose Lyris, long video generation framework in which vision-language model authors the layout of unseen regions before video model generates them. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse: 3D layout with one labeled bounding box per object [22, 58, 79] is simple enough for vision-language model to author (and for user to edit), yet expressive enough for video model to follow. We fine-tune pretrained video diffusion model to follow renderings of this layout, which specify what appears where and anchor the camera to its path, even in unseen regions. To remain consistent upon return, we reconstruct each generated chunk and write it into persistent point-cloud memory, which conditions every subsequent chunk alongside the layout. The resulting loop between explicit 3D geometry and photorealistic video generation extends the walkthrough far beyond the photo, as the layout and the memory condition each chunk, and each generated chunk in turn extends the memory from which the next layout is planned. We make the following contributions: We present Lyris, long video generation framework that pairs 3D layout of unseen regions planned by visionlanguage model with persistent 3D memory of existing ones, enabling consistent 3D world exploration from as little as single image without human authoring. We demonstrate that the layout is crucial for camera control in unseen regions, and that rendering it into the target views is far more effective than stating it in the text prompt. We outperform state-of-the-art methods on minute-long round trips across four datasets, reducing camera error by 3.8 and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average. 2. Related Work Camera-controlled video generation. Video diffusion models [28] generate photorealistic clips [8, 60, 73, 81] and increasingly accept multimodal conditions [51, 52, 56]. To control the viewpoint, existing methods inject per-frame camera poses [71] or dense Plucker ray embeddings [26, 77], often through dedicated conditioning branches [1, 2], and extend beyond single clips by conditioning each new clip on frames of the preceding one [27]. Geometry-guided approaches instead condition on point-cloud renderings at the target views [10, 54, 87, 88], couple implicit reconstruction of the input views with generation [39], or repair renderings of imperfect reconstructions [14, 74]. These methods guide generation where geometry has been observed, but leave the content of unobserved regions to the generative prior. SpatialCrafter [19] instead generates the geometry of these regions with 3D generator conditioned on the input image alone, whereas Lyris lays them out as labeled boxes that vision-language model can write and user can edit. Scene memory for long video generation. To generate long videos, memory-based methods condition each new frame or chunk on previously observed or generated content. Many approaches compress this history into limited token budget [11, 29, 72, 92] or retrieve its most relevant parts [41, 76, 82, 86]. However, the model must still infer how this history maps to the target view, which often fails under large viewpoint changes [57]. second line of work addresses this by aligning the history with the target camera before generation [13, 57, 89, 90], or by maintaining scene geometry that is rendered into the target views [12, 33, 49, 54, 59, 75, 94, 95]. Although rendering aligns the memory with each target view, errors can accumulate in the geometry itself [49, 59, 94]. Other methods instead generate and simulate an editable latent 3D scene around the agent, albeit trained with ground-truth 3D supervision in voxel game [24], or sample all views jointly in geometry-native latent space [47]. Whatever its form, however, memory of past frames preserves what has already been seen but offers nothing beyond it. There, the camera can only be conveyed through pose encodings [57, 90], which control it far less precisely than rendered geometry [10, 54]. The content, in turn, is left to the text prompt. Lyris also maintains an explicit point-cloud memory, but pairs it with 3D layout of the objects that unseen regions Figure 2. Overview of Lyris. To decide what lies beyond the input views, we use vision-language model to plan 3D layout of labeled object boxes before each chunk k. We then render this layout and our point-cloud memory at its cameras Ck to guide the video model. The memory video preserves what has been seen, while the layout video specifies what appears where beyond it and anchors the camera to its path. To remain consistent upon return, we reconstruct each generated chunk and write it into the memory. should contain. Rendered into the same target views, this layout anchors the camera where the memory is empty and leaves the appearance of these objects, but no longer their placement, to the generative prior. As the generated views follow their requested cameras more closely, they also align more reliably with the memory, limiting the errors that accumulate in its geometry. Layout-conditioned generation. Scene structure is an effective control signal when it is available in advance. Generative renderers turn animated proxy meshes [9], 3D tracking videos [25], coarse geometry [36], or depth rendered by game engine [50] into realistic or stylized video. Although some remain consistent even when region is revisited [25, 50], they all require this structure to be modeled or captured beforehand. Looser controls ease this requirement by specifying mainly where content should appear, as boxes for images [5] or short video clips [6, 65, 67]. Layoutguided methods similarly generate entire indoor scenes from 3D layouts [18, 55, 78] and street scenes from road maps and object boxes [4, 23, 48, 52] or street and height maps [15]. However, these controls are typically authored by hand or taken from an existing scene or map, which does not scale to open-ended exploration. Lyris instead conditions on coarse object layout that vision-language model writes for unseen regions, along with persistent memory that keeps revisited regions consistent. Language-driven scene planning. Large language and vision-language models have emerged as effective planners for visual content. Many systems use them to lay out 3D scenes [7, 16, 22, 44, 58, 79, 91], but these scenes inherit the synthetic appearance of the assets and engines that realize them. Other methods instead direct generative models through language, describing the content to generate next [17, 85] or iteratively refining prompts or plans for video generation [46, 80]. Although this avoids synthetic appearance, their plans remain natural language, which can name content but only coarsely describe where it belongs. Lyris bridges the two: vision-language model authors 3D layout of labeled boxes, and video diffusion model turns it into photorealistic video. Closest to our work, recent methods also guide video models with 3D boxes that language model plans or programs [35, 37, 64]. However, these boxes direct individual objects and leave the scene around them to the video model, whereas ours lay out the scene beyond the capture. Concurrent to our work, AgiWorld [20] also plans unseen regions with languagemodel agent, but conveys its layout through the text prompt, strategy that we find far less effective than rendering the layout (Sec. 4.4). CoDeR [21] instead re-creates the entire scene in code, which only approximates what the input image shows, whereas we keep the captured scene and lay out what lies beyond it. 3. Method Given one or few input views, camera path, and an optional text description of what each part of the path should reveal, our goal is to generate long video that follows the path far beyond the observed regions, while remaining consistent when the camera returns. Our solution is chunkwise autoregressive video model guided by 3D layout of labeled object boxes, which vision-language model plans for unseen regions, and by persistent point-cloud memory and appearance references. We describe our object layouts in Sec. 3.1, our scene memory in Sec. 3.2, and our video model and its training in Sec. 3.3. Figure 2 illustrates our overall approach. Figure 3. Layout planning. To keep the layout consistent with the observed scene, the vision-language model first fits boxes to the objects visible in the input view (a). It then adds box for every object that the chunks should reveal, following their descriptions (b). To ensure that the layout is physically plausible and visible along the path, we verify the proposal with geometric checks (c) and revise the boxes they flag from their proposed positions (dashed in b) to their final ones. The video model then generates each object where its box places it, such as the vase, which was moved into view (d). 3.1. Object Layouts Layout representation. We represent the layout as set = {bi} of labeled 3D bounding boxes, one per object, where each box bi is parameterized by its center ci R3, size si R3, rotation θi about the gravity axis, and text label. The boxes determine what unseen regions contain and where, and leave the shape and appearance of each object to the video model. As each box is tied to single object, user can also change what is generated by moving or relabeling boxes before generation  (Fig. 6)  . Planning. To let the layout build on what has already been generated, we use vision-language model to plan the layout [22, 58, 79] of what each chunk will reveal right before it is generated  (Fig. 3)  . The planner receives the chunks start frame, the point-cloud memory, the boxes of earlier chunks, and the chunks cameras, and thus does not require the full camera path in advance. To keep the layout consistent with the existing scene, it first estimates rectangular floor plan that encloses the memorys points and the chunks cameras and fits boxes to the objects visible in the start frame (Fig. 3a). It then determines which objects the chunk should reveal, following its description when one is given, and adds box for each, placing it relative to the existing boxes and within the floor plan. Verification. To ensure that the layout is physically plausible and visible along the path, we verify the proposal with geometric checks (Fig. 3c). The checks test whether each box is supported, lies within the floor plan and outside observed free space, does not collide with other boxes, is visible from the planned cameras, and satisfies the spatial relations of its description. We then let the model revise its proposal once, given the violations and renderings of the layout from above and from the planned cameras, and resolve the remaining violations with deterministic repair (Fig. 3b). We provide details in the supplement. Layout video and text prompt. We condition the video model on the layout through layout video, which renders the boxes of objects yet to be generated from each chunks cameras Ck. The layout video shows where each object belongs in every frame and anchors the camera to its path, even in unseen regions. To indicate what each box contains, we render it in color unique to its label and name the object of each color in the text prompt (e.g., the light violet box is long table in Fig. 2). 3.2. Scene Memory As the video model keeps no state across chunks, we maintain scene memory of everything observed or generated so far, as colored point cloud and bank of posed frames. We initialize it by reconstructing the input views [38, 68, 69]. Memory video. To show the video model what the scene already contains, we render the point cloud from each chunks cameras Ck, as in prior geometry-conditioned video models [12, 54, 95], and provide the resulting memory video as reference video. Appearance references. As point renderings lack fine detail, we also provide few frames of as reference images. We select the frames whose views overlap the most with the chunks cameras, similar to Lyra2 [57], and provide details in the supplement. Memory update. To let later chunks build on what has been generated, we add each chunk to the memory once it is complete. We reconstruct subset of its frames with Pi3X [68, 69] together with frames of the previous chunk, and align the reconstruction to the memory with similarity transform fitted on these shared frames [63]. To keep misaligned geometry out of the memory, we accept the update only if the aligned cameras deviate from the requested ones by at most 15 in rotation and quarter of their spread in translation. We then add the new points to and the frames to H. chunk that fails this test remains in the video but leaves the memory unchanged. Layout update. To keep the layout consistent with what has been generated, we then update it against the memory. We exclude the boxes of objects that the point cloud now shows in full from the layout video, and refit the boxes of partially generated objects to their points, so that the remainder of each object continues the part that exists. All other boxes remain as planned. vision-language model is more effective than leaving it purely to the video model. We validate the contribution of individual components and measure how closely Lyris follows its layouts in Sec. 4.4. 3.3. Video Model 4.1. Setup Model. We start from pretrained bidirectional video diffusion model (MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [51]), freeze its VAE and Qwen3-VL encoder [3], and fine-tune its transformer with LoRA [30] via the original flow matching objective [45]. As the model natively supports reference images and videos, we provide the layout and memory videos as reference videos and the appearance references as reference images. Prefix frame. To maintain temporal coherence across chunks, each chunk starts from prefix frame: an input view for the first chunk, and the last frame of the previous chunk for every other. The prefix frame also serves as an additional appearance reference. The supplement describes how we stabilize the transitions between chunks at inference. Camera embedding. The memory and layout videos convey the camera motion only where they show content. To provide camera control even when both are entirely empty, we encode the cameras Ck as Plucker rays [26] and add them to the tokens of the target and reference frames via linear layer in each transformer block. We zero-initialize these layers to ensure compatibility and stability with the pretrained initialization. Training. We construct training examples from captured clips of ScanNet++ [83] and DL3DV [43], treating each clip as one chunk and its first frame as the prefix frame. We render the memory video from geometry estimated from the input views instead of ground truth, so that the model must learn to handle the incomplete coverage and reconstruction artifacts that it encounters at inference. We derive the layout video from the 3D instance annotations of ScanNet++, using the boxes of objects visible beyond the first frame, and omit it for DL3DV clips, which provide no such annotations. We also drop the memory and layout videos independently with probability 0.2 each (and the text prompt with probability 0.1), so that single model can generate from any subset of these conditions. 4. Experiments As our goal is to extend captured scenes well beyond what was observed while remaining consistent upon return, we evaluate Lyris on long round-trip trajectories. We first give every method the same detailed description of what lies ahead, and assess how well each generates it (Sec. 4.2). Exploring new scene usually comes without such descriptions, so in Sec. 4.3, we only provide the caption of the start frame, and we assess whether planning what lies ahead with Implementation. We fine-tune MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [51] with rank-32 LoRA on its attention and feed-forward layers, using 124-frame clips at 832 480 resolution from 9,926 DL3DV-10K [43] and 747 ScanNet++ v2 [83] scenes (the latter of which provide object annotations). We train on clips that start from one to five input views for 1,500 iterations using AdamW with learning rate of 104 on 128 H100 GPUs. We then add clips that continue from previous one for another 500 iterations (so that the model learns to build on its memory and retrieved references), and distill the resulting model into few-step student via DMD2 [84]. We use MoGe-3 [38] to lift single frames, Pi3X [68, 69] to reconstruct multiple frames, GPT-6 to caption the training clips, and Claude Opus 5.5 to plan layouts. At test time, we retrieve three appearance references per chunk and sample with eight steps and no guidance. We provide more details in the supplement. Round trips. Each round trip follows the cameras of real capture for up to 372 frames on the way out and retraces them on the way back, for total of up to 744 frames, or about one minute of video at 12 fps. On average, the start frame observes only 29% of the pixels on the way out, leaving the rest to be generated, and the way back tests whether method remembers what it generated there. In the directed setting (Sec. 4.2), every method receives detailed description of each 124-frame window of the path, written by GPT6 from the captured video, and in the autonomous setting (Sec. 4.3) only caption of the start frame. All evaluation scenes are held out from training. Baselines. We compare Lyris to recent video generation methods that differ in how they leverage memory, namely AnyRecon [12], GEN3C [54], and Spatia [95], which condition on point-cloud renderings, Lyra2 [57], which instead establishes dense correspondences to history frames through per-frame geometry, and WorldCrafter [89], which queries an implicit 3D-aware memory. We also compare to SolarWM-H3 [32], camera-controlled world model that builds on MiniMax-H3 as we do. All six baselines leave unseen regions directly to the video model. We run the official code of each method with its default settings and the same start frame, cameras, and text as Lyris (except for AnyRecon, whose official code uses an empty prompt). Metrics. Directed Layouts Datasets. We evaluate on ScanNet++ [83] and CA-1M [40] as real indoor captures with LiDAR depth and 3D object annotations, which we use in Sec. 4.4 to measure how closely Lyris follows its layouts. We test on 20 held-out scenes of the former and the 20 longest landscape captures of the latter, which Lyris is not trained on. We provide additional results on DL3DV-Evaluation [43] (not overlapping with DL3DV-10K scenes) and from sparse input views in the supplement. Results. We summarize our results in Tab. 1 and show qualitative comparison in Fig. 4. We again test on 20 scenes of each and provide additional details in the supplement. Results. We present quantitative results, using the same metrics as Tab. 1, in Tab. 2, and qualitative results in Fig. 5. Lyris outperforms all baselines on every metric on all four datasets. Ablation and Diagnostics Components. We ablate our design decisions by individthe ually omitting the major components of our method: layout, the memorys point cloud, and the appearance references. We summarize our results in Tab. 3. The layout is crucial, as omitting it increases the rotation error roughly threeto sevenfold and lowers consistency upon return, both with or without description. Stating the layout only in the prompt, as the planners natural-language description of each chunk, instead of rendering it is far less effective, with 2.8 higher rotation error. Omitting the memorys point cloud degrades every metric, whereas omitting the appearance references mainly lowers consistency upon return. Lyris also remains ahead of all baselines in camera accuracy and consistency upon return with smaller planner (Claude Haiku 5.5), an open-weight one (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next), or the smaller Cosmos3-Nano [52] as its video model. Layout Editing As our layout consists of one labeled box per object, user can directly edit it to control what Lyris generates. In unseen regions, the boxes determine what is generated and where, and moving, swapping, or adding them changes the content accordingly  (Fig. 6)  . In the existing scene, objects are also stored in our memory, which we thus edit along with the layout. As this memory is an explicit point cloud, we simply move an objects points together with its box, and hide the points that new box occludes. Although Lyris is trained only on static scenes, we find that moving box over time also moves its object in the generated video (e.g., chair sliding away from wall or ball rolling across the floor). We illustrate each of these edits on our project page. B. Method Details B.1. Planner output. We show three of the boxes that the planner adds in the second chunk of CA-1M round trip, without their colors and justifications. Each box is fully specified by label, center and size in meters, and rotation about the gravity axis in degrees. Planning. We use Claude Opus 5.5 as our planner, although Lyris also outperforms all baselines with smaller and openweight planners (Sec. A.2). As our layout only requires one labeled box per object, we simply query the planner with fixed prompts, without tools or fine-tuning. It first localizes each object visible in the start frame with 2D bounding box, which we lift to 3D by fitting box to the memory Table 11. Geometric checks. We verify each box that the planner proposes with the six checks of Sec. 3.1. Their tolerances are the same for every scene and dataset. Check box passes if Support Floor plan Free space Collisions Visibility Relations it rests on the floor (within 0.15 m), on another box, or on the memorys points, or hangs on wall its center lies inside the floor plan at most 25% of it lies in space that the start frame observes to be empty at most 5% of the smaller of two boxes lies inside the other, or no more than for annotated objects of their classes in our training scenes (e.g., chair under table) at least 2,000 of its pixels (500 for objects smaller than 0.6 m) are unoccluded in at least 20% of the chunks frames it satisfies the spatial relations that its description states points within it. To place the objects that the chunk should reveal, we render the point-cloud memory and the fitted boxes from above and from four of the chunks cameras, overlaid with metric grid so that the planner can specify each new box in metric coordinates  (Fig. 8)  . Similar to LayoutGPT [22], we retrieve two layouts with matching objects from the annotated ScanNet++ scenes of our training set as in-context examples, and provide median object sizes. Verification. We sample five proposals and verify each with the six geometric checks of Sec. 3.1, whose criteria we list in Tab. 11. We select the proposal with the fewest violations and let the planner revise it once, after which the deterministic repair resolves the remaining violations by displacing each flagged box as little as possible. Finally, we remove the placed boxes that are still not visible, collide with another box, or contradict stated relation. The checks use the same tolerances for every scene and dataset. They are mainly for gross errors, and their exact values are not critical, as Lyris is robust to imprecise boxes. Even when we perturb the final boxes with Gaussian noise (standard deviations of up to 0.3 m, 25%, and 20 in position, size, and orientation), the rotation error on the directed CA-1M round trips increases by less than 1, and Lyris still outperforms all baselines on every metric of Tab. 1. Autonomous setting. Given only caption of the input view, the planner itself decides which objects each chunk should reveal, and writes the chunks description from the resulting layout. When the full camera path is available before generation (Lyris w/ full path in Tab. 2), it instead plans the layout for the whole path at once, from the input views and the cameras of all chunks. B.2. Layout Rendering and Update Rendering. As the text prompt refers to each box by its color, we render the boxes of each training clip in perceptually distinct named colors, which we sample at random for each clip. As each training clip contains at most 12 boxes, we likewise render at most 12 boxes per chunk at inference, and sample palette of 12 colors once per path. Each label thus retains its color across chunks, and path with more than 12 labels reuses colors across chunks while keeping those within each chunk distinct. Update. As the memory video already shows what has been generated, the layout video prioritizes rendering only what has not. Before each subsequent chunk, we thus measure how much of each object the memory contains, as the fraction of its boxs pixels that are covered by memory points inside the box. Above 0.8, we consider the object fully generated and exclude its box. Between 0.1 and 0.8, we consider it partially generated and refit its box to the largest cluster of memory points around it, so that the remainder of the object continues the part that exists. As this cluster can include neighboring surfaces (e.g., the wall behind the object), we preserve the orientation of the box and allow each side to grow by at most 1.5. Otherwise, the object is yet to be generated and its box remains as planned. When more than 12 boxes remain, we prioritize those planned in unseen regions over those fitted to visible objects, as the prefix frame already shows the latter. B.3. Reference Retrieval From the bank of input views and previously generated frames, we retrieve up to three appearance references per chunk, selected to maximize their joint coverage of the chunks views. For each frame in H, we project its estimated depth into every eighth camera of the chunk to obtain the set Vi of pixels that it observes, with depth test for occlusion. As each chunk already receives its prefix frame, we initialize the selection with it and greedily add the frame that maximizes the additional coverage, = arg max /R (cid:12) (cid:12)Vi (cid:83) jR Vj (cid:12) (cid:12). (1) Once no frame increases the coverage, we select the remaining references by the proximity of their cameras to the chunks. When chunk returns close to the start of the path, we additionally include the first input view, so that the chunk is conditioned on the captured view itself. B.4. Memory Update We initialize the memory with the monocular depth [38] of the first input view, and reconstruct any further input views jointly with Pi3X [68, 69]. As errors in this memory would persist for the rest of the video, we align each chunk to it, add only the points that are reliable and not yet contained in it, and discard the update altogether if the alignment deviates from the requested cameras. Alignment. We reconstruct every eighth frame of the chunk with Pi3X, conditioned on the requested cameras, together with frames that the memory already contains, and fit similarity transform [63] to the 3D points of these shared frames. With single input view, the first chunk shares no reconstructed frame with the memory, and we instead fit the transform to its camera centers. As these alone can misestimate the scale, we then rescale the reconstruction to the depth of the input view. Filtering. From each reconstructed frame, we first discard the points with low Pi3X confidence or at depth discontinuities, where the reconstruction is least reliable. To keep single copy of each surface, we then render the current point cloud into the frames camera and discard the points whose depth agrees with the rendered depth within relative tolerance. We likewise discard the points that lie on or in front of the surfaces observed by the first input view, as they would duplicate or contradict this captured view, and add the remaining points to P. To ensure that the memory video still covers the entire prefix frame of the next chunk, we also lift this frame with monocular depth, scaled to the memory, and render its points wherever the memory provides none. Acceptance test. We accept the update only if the median rotation between the aligned and the requested cameras is at most 15 and the root-mean-square error of their centers is at most 0.25 times the cameras spread, i.e., the rootmean-square distance of the centers from their mean. As this spread vanishes when the camera turns in place, we use 0.2 times the median depth of the new frames instead whenever it is larger. On the directed CA-1M round trips, 93% of the updates pass this test, against 78% without the layout, as the generated cameras then follow the requested ones less closely. B.5. Chunk Transitions We generate 124 frames per chunk and keep the first 107 (all but the last latent group of the video VAE, which has the lowest imaging quality), continuing the next chunk from the last frame that we keep. As the model is trained with captured prefix frames, we sharpen this generated frame with an unsharp mask (radius of 2 pixels, amount of 70%) before it conditions the next chunk, while the output video retains the original frame. In the first chunk, we also replace the latents that the memory video covers with its own (noised to the current level) after each of the first two of the eight sampling steps, which keeps the chunk aligned with the input views. These choices slightly improve consistency upon return and imaging quality (by 0.026 and 1.5 on the directed CA-1M round trips of Tab. 1, and by 0.021 and 1.4 on those of ScanNet++). Without them, Lyris still outperforms all baselines in camera accuracy, consistency upon return, and imaging quality. B.6. Architecture To preserve the prior of the pretrained model, we keep the architecture of MiniMax-H3 unchanged apart from the camFigure 9. Video model. The DiT processes the latents of the noisy target together with those of the memory video, the prefix frame and appearance references, and the layout video, and with the Qwen3-VL embedding of the text prompt, through joint selfattention. We freeze the VAE and Qwen3-VL, fine-tune the DiT with LoRA, and add only zero-initialized linear layer per block that embeds the cameras Ck as Plucker rays. era embedding, and provide all other conditions through its native reference inputs  (Fig. 9)  . The VAE latents of these conditions thus enter the joint self-attention of the DiT as separate tokens, while the Qwen3-VL encoder embeds their frames together with the text prompt. As the prefix frame is the first frame of the chunk, its tokens share the RoPE positions of the first target frame, whereas the appearance references keep separate positions. For the camera embedding, we compute one Plucker ray per latent position, relative to the first target camera, averaging the cameras over the frames that each latent frame compresses. Each target and reference-image token receives its rays at the self-attention input of every transformer block, through linear layer that we zero-initialize so that training starts from the pretrained model. B.7. Training and Distillation Training. The two stages of Sec. 4.1 expose the model to each situation that it faces at inference. Both stages use the optimizer of Sec. 4.1, with gradient clipping at 1.0 and one clip per GPU. The first stage (1,500 iterations on 128 GPUs) covers first chunks, with an even mix of ScanNet++ clips and DL3DV clips that start from one to five input views. In the second stage (500 iterations on 64 GPUs), 42.5% of the clips continue from captured previous chunk, from which we build their memory and retrieve their references as at inference. To cover returns, 20% play this previous chunk back in reverse and 12.5% do the same for an earlier chunk. The remaining 25% are first-stage clips, which keeps first chunks in the training distribution. Condition dropout. We represent memory video that is dropped during training (Sec. 3.3) by the VAE encoding of an all-gray sequence, as for memory without points. We omit dropped layout video together with the part of the prompt that names its boxes. When we drop the text prompt, we retain the Qwen3-VL embeddings of the reference images and videos, so that classifier-free guidance acts on the text prompt alone. Distillation. To sample with only eight steps and without classifier-free guidance, we distill the second-stage model with DMD2 [84] on its training clips for 500 iterations on 32 GPUs, using it as the teacher at guidance scale of 3. Every fifth iteration updates the student (learning rate 105), and the others update the fake score model (a LoRA, learning rate 104). C. Evaluation Protocol C.1. Evaluation Scenes We select the DL3DV and SpatialVID scenes of Tab. 2 from the captured footage and its metadata alone, independently of any methods output. For DL3DV, we use DL3DVEvaluation [43], separately released test split2 that does not overlap with the DL3DV-10K scenes we train on. As our task is walkthrough at natural pace from single image, we exclude scenes with very fast camera motion and those whose start frame is dominated by dense vegetation, which leaves no clear path to walk through. We then randomly sample 20 of the remaining scenes (16 indoor and 4 outdoor). As the annotated clips of SpatialVID [66] last at most 15 s, which is too short for our round trips, we instead use its long raw videos (one clip per video) and estimate their cameras with ViPE [31]. From these in-the-wild videos, we only keep ground-level walkthroughs of real, static scenes without overlaid text. To ensure that camera errors are meaningful, we further require that DA3 [42], with which we measure them, recovers the ViPE cameras from the captured footage to within 10. For fair comparison, we also require enough sparse points in the start frame to calibrate the scale of the input cameras (Sec. C.3), and exclude the footage that SolarWM-H3 [32] is trained on. The 20 videos that pass all criteria (17 indoor and 3 outdoor) form our test set. 2https : / / huggingface . co / datasets / DL3DV / DL3DV - Evaluation C.2. Metrics We score each method from its generated frames alone, without access to its internal cameras or geometry. As the way back retraces the way out, we measure Revisit across the two and all other metrics on the way out, and average each over scenes. Camera accuracy. As every method starts from the same frame, we align the cameras that DA33 recovers from each generated video with the input cameras at this frame only, such that the errors include any drift along the path, and fit single scale to the recovered positions. Observed pixels. To restrict PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS to the pixels that the start frame observes, we determine these pixels from the capture, such that they are identical for every method. pixel is observed if its captured surface reprojects into the start frame within relative depth tolerance of 10%, using the captured depth of CA-1M and ScanNet++ and MoGe-3 [38] depth scaled to the sparse points of DL3DV and SpatialVID. Consistency upon return. Revisit compares the two frames generated at each revisited camera directly, as the cosine similarity of their DINOv2-large patch features. We exclude the cameras that are revisited within 48 frames (around the turn), as frames this close in time remain consistent without memory. Objects. As the judge should favor no method, we use Gemini 3.1 Pro at temperature 0 (a model that neither plans our layouts nor writes the descriptions), and withhold the name of the method. We ask it which of the objects that each description names (as extracted by GPT-6) appear in 31 evenly spaced frames of the way out. D. Limitations As Lyris builds its memory from estimated geometry, depth and alignment errors can accumulate over very long paths. Our acceptance test (Sec. B.4) discards unreliable updates, and stronger reconstruction models are directly applicable to our method. Lyris does not currently model dynamic scenes, as it is trained only on static captures. However, moving box over time already moves its object in the generated video (Sec. A.8), which makes training on dynamic data promising direction. Our layout specifies only labeled box per object, and thus offers no control over its detailed shape, which richer primitives rendered into the layout video could provide. Finally, Lyris is not yet interactive, as planning and sampling run in sequence for every chunk, which faster planners and distillation into causal model [14] could address. E. Societal Impact Lyris generates explorable environments from as little as single photo, which benefits applications such as virtual touring, content creation, and simulation for physical AI. Its explicit layout further allows user to inspect and edit what will be generated before any frame is rendered. However, as Lyris plausibly extends real places beyond what was captured, it raises concerns about potential misuse for generating deceptive visual media (e.g., presenting generated walkthrough as real footage). Although Lyris is trained on static scenes and is not designed to synthesize people, appropriate safeguards such as watermarking generated content should be considered for deployment. As Lyris builds on pretrained video model and vision-language planner, it also inherits the biases of their training data (e.g., toward common room types and furnishings).
